---
title: "Center Buildout Capacity"
subtitle: "Daybreak, Saratoga Springs Downtown, and The Point"
---

## Purpose

For three WCV centers -- Daybreak, Saratoga Springs Downtown, and The Point
-- this answers three questions per center:

1. **Current year (2025)** homes and jobs -- where things stand today.
2. **2055 forecast** homes and jobs -- REMM's own simulated outcome by 2055.
3. **Full REMM capacity** homes and jobs -- see `## Full REMM capacity`
   below; the method differs by center, since The Point's is already fully
   built out by 2055 per REMM (nothing developable left), while Daybreak and
   Saratoga Springs Downtown still have land redeveloping past 2025 whose
   *additional* capacity has to be estimated from density assumptions.

Metrics 1 and 2 use one shared calculation for all three centers. See
`## Summary` for the combined results and CSV exports (chart pending).

Spatial joins, filtering, and aggregation below run in geopandas/pandas.
The base-year parcels come from `remm_base_year_data.gdb`, which is cached
as GeoParquet on first run (see below) so later runs just read that instead
of re-parsing the FileGDB.

## Centers of interest

Single ordered list to extend if more centers are added later.
`center_boundaries` is fetched in full from the REST service (no
server-side `where`), so adding a center here doesn't require touching
`sources.yml` or re-fetching -- just delete `_data/processed/centers.parquet`
to force it to rebuild with the updated list.

Every `gpd.read_file()` call below passes an OGR SQL `where` built straight
from that list, restricted to "Urban Center" polygons (drops The Point's
separate "Employment District" polygon, since every center in scope for
this analysis is its Urban Center polygon).

```{python}
CENTERS_OF_INTEREST = ["Daybreak", "Saratoga Springs Downtown", "The Point"]
```

## Load center boundaries

```{python}
from gis_adhoc_analyses.layer_cache import ensure_layers
import geopandas as gpd

L = ensure_layers(["center_boundaries"])
centers_preview = gpd.read_file(
    L["center_boundaries"],
    where=f"CenterName IN ({', '.join(map(repr, CENTERS_OF_INTEREST))}) AND CenterType = 'Urban Center'",
)
centers_preview[["CenterName", "CenterType", "City", "DwellingPerAcre", "NonResFAR"]]
```

```{python}
#| eval: false
centers_preview.explore(

```

## REMM parcels: load and cache as parquet

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd

paths = {
    "raw": Path("_data/raw"),
    "processed": Path("_data/processed"),
}
paths["processed"].mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

paths.update({
    "gdb": paths["raw"] / "remm" / "remm_base_year_data.gdb",
    "buildings_2055_pkl": paths["raw"] / "remm" / "run1842year2055allbuildings.pkl",
    "progression_2055_pkl": paths["raw"] / "remm" / "run_1842_year_2055_parcel_progression_metrics.pkl",
    "parcels_geoparquet": paths["processed"] / "parcels_2023.parquet",
    "centers_geoparquet": paths["processed"] / "centers.parquet",
    "buildings_2055_parquet": paths["processed"] / "buildings_2055.parquet",
    "progression_2055_parquet": paths["processed"] / "progression_2055.parquet",
})

# one-time read of the two vector sources, cached as GeoParquet so later runs
# don't re-parse the FileGDB or re-fetch the REST layer. Each cache is a full
# replica of every source column -- selecting only the columns actually
# needed for a given step happens later, at read time (via `columns=`), not
# by trimming what gets cached here.
if not paths["parcels_geoparquet"].exists():
    parcels_gdf = gpd.read_file(paths["gdb"], layer="parcels")
    # Split_Factor/MAG_parcel_id mix strings with a couple of real NaNs, which
    # pyarrow can't write as a single column type -- nullable string dtype
    # keeps those as actual nulls (not the literal string "nan").
    parcels_gdf["Split_Factor"] = parcels_gdf["Split_Factor"].astype("string")
    parcels_gdf["MAG_parcel_id"] = parcels_gdf["MAG_parcel_id"].astype("string")
    parcels_gdf.to_parquet(paths["parcels_geoparquet"])

if not paths["centers_geoparquet"].exists():
    centers_gdf = gpd.read_file(
        L["center_boundaries"],
        where=f"CenterName IN ({', '.join(map(repr, CENTERS_OF_INTEREST))}) AND CenterType = 'Urban Center'",
    )
    centers_gdf.to_parquet(paths["centers_geoparquet"])

if not paths["buildings_2055_parquet"].exists():
    buildings_full = pd.read_pickle(paths["buildings_2055_pkl"]).reset_index()
    # 'note' mixes real strings with an int 0 sentinel (no dedicated null),
    # which pyarrow can't write as a single column type. 0 means "no note", so
    # it's replaced with an actual null rather than becoming the string "0".
    buildings_full["note"] = buildings_full["note"].replace(0, pd.NA).astype("string")
    buildings_full.to_parquet(paths["buildings_2055_parquet"])

if not paths["progression_2055_parquet"].exists():
    # no mixed-type columns here, so a plain conversion is enough
    pd.read_pickle(paths["progression_2055_pkl"]).to_parquet(paths["progression_2055_parquet"])

# only the columns needed for the spatial join below (geometry + acreage/name) --
# other columns (max_far, max_dua, DwellingPerAcre, ...) get pulled later, from
# the same cached files, only where they're actually used.
parcels = gpd.read_parquet(paths["parcels_geoparquet"], columns=["parcel_id", "parcel_acres", "geometry"])
centers = gpd.read_parquet(
    paths["centers_geoparquet"], columns=["CenterName", "CenterType", "geometry"]
).to_crs(parcels.crs)  # centers ships in EPSG:4326 (WGS84) from the REST layer; parcels are in EPSG:26912 (UTM 12N)
```

## Parcels within each center

Centroid-in-polygon join (not a straight intersection) so a parcel
straddling a center boundary is assigned to exactly one center, not
double-counted.

```{python}
# swap each parcel's polygon for its centroid point -- a polygon can legitimately
# intersect two centers along a shared edge, but its centroid falls in exactly one.
parcel_centroids = parcels.set_geometry(parcels.geometry.centroid)

# predicate="within": keep a parcel only if its centroid point falls inside a
# center polygon. how="inner" drops parcels whose centroid falls in no center
# at all (most of the region -- centers are a tiny fraction of all parcels).
parcels_in_centers = gpd.sjoin(
    parcel_centroids, centers[["CenterName", "geometry"]], predicate="within", how="inner"
)[["parcel_id", "parcel_acres", "CenterName"]]

parcels_per_center = parcels_in_centers.groupby("CenterName").agg(
    n_parcels=("parcel_id", "count"), total_acres=("parcel_acres", "sum")
)
parcels_per_center
```

```{python}
# parcels within our 3 centers of interest, reused by every metric below.
# parcels_in_centers already only contains parcels inside Daybreak, Saratoga
# Springs Downtown, and The Point (centers.parquet was itself built from the
# 3-row where-filtered fetch) -- this isin() is a defensive, explicit filter
# so downstream cells don't silently depend on that upstream scoping.
our_parcels = parcels_in_centers[parcels_in_centers["CenterName"].isin(CENTERS_OF_INTEREST)]
```

## Metric 1: current year (2025) homes and jobs

No dedicated 2025 REMM run exists (only "2023" and "2055" pickles), so this
derives 2025 by filtering the 2055 run's buildings table
(`run1842year2055allbuildings.pkl`, one row per *building*) to
`year_built <= 2025` and summing `residential_units`/`job_spaces` per
center. One shared calculation for all three centers.

**Data quality note:** filtering to `year_built <= 2023` instead reproduces
the dedicated `run1842year2023allbuildings.pkl` exactly for Daybreak (905
units/2,389 jobs) and Saratoga Springs Downtown (0/0), but not for The Point
(2023 pickle: 0 units/2,474 jobs vs. 2055-run-filtered: 0/978) -- the two
REMM runs disagree on The Point's historical baseline. Proceeding with the
uniform `year_built <= 2025` method regardless: The Point was a state
prison site until recently, so a real drop from ~2,474 jobs (2023,
pre-closure) to ~978 (2025, post-closure/pre-redevelopment) is a plausible
read, not necessarily a data error -- consistent with satellite imagery
showing The Point still mostly undeveloped today.

```{python}
buildings_2055 = pd.read_parquet(
    paths["buildings_2055_parquet"],
    columns=["parcel_id", "year_built", "general_type", "residential_units", "job_spaces"],
)

current_year = (
    buildings_2055[buildings_2055["year_built"] <= 2025]
    .merge(our_parcels[["parcel_id", "CenterName"]], on="parcel_id")
    .groupby("CenterName")[["residential_units", "job_spaces"]]
    .sum()
    .rename(columns={"residential_units": "homes", "job_spaces": "jobs"})
)
current_year
```

## Metric 2: 2055 forecast homes and jobs

REMM's own simulated outcome by 2055 -- sum `parcel_progression_metrics`'s
`residential_units`/`job_spaces` (verified reliable per-parcel sums across
all of a parcel's buildings, unlike `year_built`, which only reflects one
representative building) across **all** parcels in each center, not just
the ones that redevelop after 2025. Same shared calculation for all three
centers -- this is exactly what The Point's full-buildout figure below
already is, since REMM shows nothing left developable there by 2055.

```{python}
progression_2055 = pd.read_parquet(
    paths["progression_2055_parquet"], columns=["parcel_id", "residential_units", "job_spaces"]
)

forecast_2055 = (
    our_parcels.merge(progression_2055, on="parcel_id")
    .groupby("CenterName")[["residential_units", "job_spaces"]]
    .sum()
    .rename(columns={"residential_units": "homes", "job_spaces": "jobs"})
)
forecast_2055
```

## Full REMM capacity (metric 3)

Method differs by center:

- **Daybreak & Saratoga Springs Downtown**: developable acreage (parcels
  with a building `year_built > 2025`) x forecast res/nonres mix ratio x
  median density assumptions = **additional** housing units/jobs on top of
  today's baseline (metric 1) -- not an absolute total by itself. Combined
  with metric 1 in `## Summary` to get a comparable absolute figure.
- **The Point**: no separate development schedule document was ever
  provided, and The Point is already REMM-modeled, so "the development
  schedule" here means REMM's own full-buildout simulation directly (no
  density-assumption modeling needed) -- REMM shows 0 parcels still
  developable there as of 2055, so this figure already **is** an absolute
  total, identical to its metric 2 (2055 forecast).

### Daybreak & Saratoga Springs Downtown: developable land

Follows the original pseudocode directly: filter the 2055 buildings table
to parcels within our centers of interest, keep buildings with
`year_built > 2025`, take the unique parcel ids from that, then sum
`parcel_acres` for those parcels. Computed for all three centers here too
(The Point's result is an exploratory cross-check only -- see above).

An earlier version of this shortcut off the parcel-level
`parcel_progression_metrics` table instead, since it already carries a
single `year_built` per parcel. That's only valid if every building on a
parcel always shares the same year/type -- checked directly: 162 parcels
regionwide have more than one building, 2 of them are in our centers of
interest, and in both cases the buildings on that parcel happened to share
the same `year_built`. That was a coincidence of this dataset, not
something the data guarantees in general, so this filters at the building
level as originally specified rather than relying on it holding elsewhere.

```{python}
# inner join: only buildings whose parcel_id is one of our centers' parcels survive.
buildings_in_centers = buildings_2055.merge(our_parcels[["parcel_id", "CenterName"]], on="parcel_id")

# a parcel can have multiple buildings (see note above) -- .unique() collapses
# "one row per building built after 2025" down to "one row per qualifying parcel".
post_2025_parcel_ids = buildings_in_centers.loc[
    buildings_in_centers["year_built"] > 2025, "parcel_id"
].unique()

developable_land = (
    our_parcels[our_parcels["parcel_id"].isin(post_2025_parcel_ids)]
    .groupby("CenterName")
    .agg(n_parcels=("parcel_id", "count"), dev_acres=("parcel_acres", "sum"))
    .reset_index()
)
developable_land
```

### Forecast development mix and buildout capacity

#### (1) Forecast residential : commercial/employment development ratio

Sum `residential_units` and `job_spaces` from `parcel_progression_metrics`
for the post-2025 developable parcels identified above (2055 run). Full
buildout of each center is assumed to follow this same mix, so each
center's total developable acreage is allocated between residential and
commercial/employment by this ratio.

```{python}
dev_mix = (
    our_parcels[our_parcels["parcel_id"].isin(post_2025_parcel_ids)][["parcel_id", "CenterName"]]
    .merge(progression_2055, on="parcel_id")
    .groupby("CenterName")[["residential_units", "job_spaces"]]
    .sum()
)
dev_mix["unit_job_ratio"] = dev_mix["residential_units"] / dev_mix["job_spaces"]

# res_share/nonres_share are the same ratio re-expressed as shares of a whole
# (res_share = unit_job_ratio / (unit_job_ratio + 1)) -- this is what actually
# gets multiplied against acreage below.
dev_mix["res_share"] = dev_mix["residential_units"] / (dev_mix["residential_units"] + dev_mix["job_spaces"])
dev_mix["nonres_share"] = 1 - dev_mix["res_share"]
dev_mix
```

```{python}
# split each center's total developable acreage into a residential and a
# non-residential/employment share, using the res_share/nonres_share
# computed above -- this is the "assume full buildout follows this same mix" step.
acreage_allocation = developable_land.set_index("CenterName").loc[
    CENTERS_OF_INTEREST, ["dev_acres"]
].join(dev_mix[["res_share", "nonres_share"]])
acreage_allocation["res_acres"] = acreage_allocation["dev_acres"] * acreage_allocation["res_share"]
acreage_allocation["nonres_acres"] = acreage_allocation["dev_acres"] * acreage_allocation["nonres_share"]
acreage_allocation
```

#### (2) Apply density assumptions to each acreage share

**Median dwelling-units-per-acre and FAR.** `max_far`/`max_dua` live on the
`parcels` table (per-parcel zoning capacity, not a text range), so this
takes the statistical median across *all* parcels in each center -- not
just the post-2025 developable ones, since the assumption is about the
center's overall zoned capacity, not only what's forecast to redevelop.
Josh noted REMM's own FAR/DUA-driven numbers assume a parcel develops
wall-to-wall (no roads, parking, or common space carved out), so if that
assumption changes later, override the values directly here (e.g.
`capacities.loc["Daybreak", "median_far"] = 2.0`) and rerun from this cell
down.

**Known limitation:** for Daybreak specifically, several of its post-2025
developable parcels are large master-planned "super-parcels" whose actual
REMM-simulated density (up to ~280 units/acre on parcels with a recorded
`max_dua` of just 30) far exceeds their generic zoning entitlement --
Daybreak's real approved density (high-rise towers via a specific
development agreement) isn't fully captured by the `max_far`/`max_dua`
fields. This makes the density-assumption-based capacity estimate
understate what REMM's own simulation already achieves -- visible in
`## Summary` below, where **both** Daybreak's and Saratoga Springs
Downtown's metric 3 homes figures come in *below* their metric 2 (2055
forecast) despite being meant as a ceiling on top of it. Left as-is for now
(including in the `## Plots` chart below, where it makes the nested bar
encoding render oddly for these two) pending a fix to the density
assumption itself.

```{python}
# our_parcels only has parcel_id/parcel_acres/CenterName -- pull max_far/max_dua
# from the same parcels cache (already scoped to our_parcels via the merge).
capacities = (
    our_parcels.merge(
        gpd.read_parquet(
            paths["parcels_geoparquet"], columns=["parcel_id", "max_far", "max_dua", "geometry"]
        ),
        on="parcel_id",
    )
    .groupby("CenterName")[["max_far", "max_dua"]]
    .median()
    .rename(columns={"max_far": "median_far", "max_dua": "median_dua"})
)
capacities  # The Point's median_dua is NaN -- none of its parcels have a max_dua entitlement yet; left as-is
```

**Median employment density, from FAR and a job-space assumption.**
`sqft_per_job` (needed to turn FAR-driven building sqft into a job count)
comes from each center's own non-residential buildings (all of them, not
just post-2025 -- there aren't many non-res buildings in Saratoga Springs
Downtown yet, so restricting to post-2025 only left a very thin sample).
It turns out to be a fixed constant per building `general_type` region-wide
(Office 633, Retail 374, Industrial 975, ...), so the median here reflects
each center's non-res building mix rather than sampling noise.

```{python}
buildings_full = pd.read_parquet(
    paths["buildings_2055_parquet"], columns=["parcel_id", "general_type", "sqft_per_job"]
).merge(our_parcels[["parcel_id", "CenterName"]], on="parcel_id")

# residential building types excluded here -- sqft_per_job only makes sense
# for the non-residential/employment share of buildout.
nonres_buildings = buildings_full[
    (buildings_full["CenterName"].isin(CENTERS_OF_INTEREST))
    & ~buildings_full["general_type"].isin(["SF Residential", "MF Residential"])
]
sqft_per_job = nonres_buildings.groupby("CenterName")["sqft_per_job"].median().rename("sqft_per_job")
sqft_per_job
```

#### (3) Estimate additional housing units and jobs at full buildout

```{python}
SQFT_PER_ACRE = 43_560

capacity = acreage_allocation.join(capacities[["median_dua", "median_far"]]).join(sqft_per_job)
# residential: acres x dwelling-units-per-acre = additional housing units
capacity["housing_units"] = capacity["res_acres"] * capacity["median_dua"]
# non-residential: acres x FAR x sqft/acre = total building sqft at full buildout
capacity["nonres_sqft"] = capacity["nonres_acres"] * capacity["median_far"] * SQFT_PER_ACRE
# building sqft / sqft-per-job = additional jobs
capacity["jobs"] = capacity["nonres_sqft"] / capacity["sqft_per_job"]
capacity[["dev_acres", "res_acres", "nonres_acres", "housing_units", "jobs"]]
```

### The Point: full buildout

Unlike Daybreak/Saratoga Springs Downtown, this doesn't need acreage
allocation or density assumptions: REMM's simulated buildings already give
unit/job counts directly, so this is just a sum, plus a check that
nothing's left undeveloped (rather than an estimate of it). **This is the
actual full-capacity figure for The Point** -- the developable-land/density-
assumption method above was computed for The Point too, but only as an
exploratory cross-check (see `capacity.loc["The Point"]`, which is NaN for
housing_units since none of its parcels have a `max_dua` entitlement yet).

```{python}
# residential_units/job_spaces here are absolute totals as of the 2055 run
# (not "_added" deltas) -- i.e. REMM's full-buildout state, not "new since 2025".
# developable/year_built/max_far/max_dua are pulled too, for the check below.
point_progression = pd.read_parquet(
    paths["progression_2055_parquet"],
    columns=["parcel_id", "residential_units", "job_spaces", "developable", "year_built", "max_far", "max_dua"],
)

point_parcels = parcels_in_centers[parcels_in_centers["CenterName"] == "The Point"]
point_buildout = point_parcels[["parcel_id", "parcel_acres"]].merge(point_progression, on="parcel_id")

# developable == 1 would mean "still vacant and buildable as of 2055" -- expect
# none, confirming there's no residual land to separately estimate.
still_developable = point_buildout[point_buildout["developable"] == 1]
print(f"parcels still flagged developable: {len(still_developable)}")

# parcels with no building recorded (year_built == 0) are only a gap if they
# also have real zoning capacity -- if max_far/max_dua are both 0 too, they're
# non-buildable infrastructure (roads, open space), not missed development.
unbuilt = point_buildout[point_buildout["year_built"] == 0]
print(f"parcels never built ({unbuilt['parcel_acres'].sum():.1f} acres), of which zero-capacity:",
      ((unbuilt["max_far"] == 0) & (unbuilt["max_dua"] == 0)).sum(), "/", len(unbuilt))

point_capacity = point_buildout[["residential_units", "job_spaces"]].sum().rename({
    "residential_units": "housing_units", "job_spaces": "jobs"
})
point_capacity
```

## Summary

```{python}
import numpy as np

# Full REMM capacity, as an absolute total comparable to metrics 1/2:
# Daybreak/Saratoga Springs Downtown = current year + additional capacity
# (task 2's density-assumption estimate); The Point = its own full-buildout
# sum directly (task 3), NOT the exploratory `capacity.loc["The Point"]` row.
housing_capacity = pd.Series(index=CENTERS_OF_INTEREST, dtype=float)
jobs_capacity = pd.Series(index=CENTERS_OF_INTEREST, dtype=float)
for center in ["Daybreak", "Saratoga Springs Downtown"]:
    housing_capacity[center] = current_year.loc[center, "homes"] + capacity.loc[center, "housing_units"]
    jobs_capacity[center] = current_year.loc[center, "jobs"] + capacity.loc[center, "jobs"]
housing_capacity["The Point"] = point_capacity["housing_units"]
jobs_capacity["The Point"] = point_capacity["jobs"]

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "total_acres": parcels_per_center["total_acres"],
    "housing_2025": current_year["homes"],
    "jobs_2025": current_year["jobs"],
    "housing_2055": forecast_2055["homes"],
    "jobs_2055": forecast_2055["jobs"],
    "housing_capacity": housing_capacity,
    "jobs_capacity": jobs_capacity,
}).loc[CENTERS_OF_INTEREST]
summary.index.name = "CenterName"
summary
```

**Note:** both Daybreak's `housing_capacity` (2,214 vs. `housing_2055`
7,077) and Saratoga Springs Downtown's (625 vs. 1,712) come in *below*
their own 2055 forecast -- see the "known limitation" callout above. The
density-assumption method understates real achievable density for both;
REMM's own 2055 simulation is itself evidence of what's actually achievable.
Decided to implement the `## Plots` housing chart as-is despite this (no
flooring at `max(capacity, housing_2055)`), accepting that the nested bar
encoding renders oddly for these two centers until the density assumption
itself is revisited.

}).reindex(CENTERS_OF_INTEREST)

detail.to_csv(output_dir / "center_buildout_detail.csv")
detail

### Plots

Employment only for now -- jobs is monotonic (current <= 2055 forecast <=
capacity) for all three centers, so the nested bullet-chart encoding below
works cleanly. Housing isn't yet, pending the Daybreak capacity-nesting
question above; the same chart will extend to housing once that's
resolved.

Horizontal bars, editorial styling inspired by Tanya Shapiro's ggplot work:
left-aligned bold title/subtitle, bars sorted largest-to-smallest, direct
value labels instead of relying on axis ticks, minimal chart junk (no
spines, no gridlines), and the WFRC brand's own typeface (Poppins) instead
of matplotlib's default font -- `Inter` (the brand's heading font) turned
out to only be installed as a variable font at weight 400, so `Poppins
SemiBold` (a proper static weight) carries the title/value labels instead,
keeping one cohesive typeface throughout rather than mixing families.

Each bar is a **Meter**-style nested encoding (see the `dataviz` skill:
fill = value, track = a lighter step of the same hue), extended from 2
tiers to 3, with all three values labeled (not just capacity):

- **Track** (full bar length): full REMM capacity -- lightest tint of the
  center's hue.
- **Hatch overlay** (0 to the 2055 figure): tone-on-tone diagonal texture --
  how much of that capacity REMM's own simulation reaches by 2055. Skipped
  for The Point, where 2055 forecast == capacity exactly (nothing left
  developable), to avoid labeling the same value twice.
- **Solid fill** (0 to the 2025 figure): full-saturation hue -- where things
  stand today.

Colors are 3 categorical hues from the WFRC brand's Core Palette (`blue
#036fa8`, `orange #ea7b00`, `green #007426`), chosen over the "Wasatch
Choice Center" colors since all three centers share the same `CenterType`
and would collide under that scheme. Validated with the `dataviz` skill's
`validate_palette.js` six-checks script: all pass except a contrast WARN on
orange (2.79, below 3:1) -- satisfied by the visible value labels here and
the table above, per the skill's relief rule.

```{python}
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

matplotlib.rcParams["hatch.linewidth"] = 2.2
matplotlib.rcParams["font.family"] = "Poppins"

CENTER_COLORS = {
    "Daybreak": "#036fa8",
    "Saratoga Springs Downtown": "#ea7b00",
    "The Point": "#007426",
}
CENTER_LABELS = {
    "Daybreak": "Daybreak",
    "Saratoga Springs Downtown": "Saratoga Springs\nDowntown",
    "The Point": "The Point",
}
SURFACE = "#fcfcfb"
TEXT_PRIMARY = "#151515"
TEXT_MUTED = "#7f7a76"
LEFT, RIGHT = 0.205, 0.92


def lighten(hex_color, amount):
    """Blend hex_color toward white by `amount` (0=no change, 1=white)."""
    hex_color = hex_color.lstrip("#")
    r, g, b = (int(hex_color[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (0, 2, 4))
    r, g, b = (int(c + (255 - c) * amount) for c in (r, g, b))
    return f"#{r:02x}{g:02x}{b:02x}"


order = summary["jobs_capacity"].sort_values(ascending=True).index.tolist()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 5.9), dpi=140)
fig.patch.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
ax.set_facecolor(SURFACE)

bar_height = 0.5
xmax = summary["jobs_capacity"].max()

for i, center in enumerate(order):
    hue = CENTER_COLORS[center]
    cap = summary.loc[center, "jobs_capacity"]
    forecast = summary.loc[center, "jobs_2055"]
    current = summary.loc[center, "jobs_2025"]

    ax.barh(i, cap, height=bar_height, color=lighten(hue, 0.8), zorder=1)
    ax.barh(i, forecast, height=bar_height, facecolor="none", hatch="///", edgecolor=lighten(hue, 0.25), linewidth=0, zorder=2)
    ax.barh(i, current, height=bar_height, color=hue, zorder=3)

    top_y = i + bar_height / 2
    if current > 0:
        ax.text(current, top_y + 0.07, f"{current:,.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=TEXT_MUTED)
    else:
        ax.text(current, top_y + 0.07, "0", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=TEXT_MUTED)
    if forecast < cap * 0.999:  # skip if 2055 == capacity (The Point) -- would duplicate the bold label
        ax.text(forecast, top_y + 0.07, f"{forecast:,.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=TEXT_MUTED)
    ax.text(cap + xmax * 0.015, i, f"{cap:,.0f}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=11, color=TEXT_PRIMARY, fontfamily="Poppins SemiBold")

ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)))
ax.set_yticklabels([CENTER_LABELS[c] for c in order], fontsize=11, color=TEXT_PRIMARY)
ax.set_xlim(0, xmax * 1.18)
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(order) - 1 + 0.75)
ax.get_xaxis().set_visible(False)

for spine in ax.spines.values():
    spine.set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)

fig.suptitle("Employment capacity across three WCV centers", x=0.03, y=0.975, fontsize=17, color=TEXT_PRIMARY, ha="left", fontfamily="Poppins SemiBold")
fig.text(0.03, 0.875, "Current jobs (2025), REMM's 2055 forecast, and full buildout capacity", fontsize=11, color=TEXT_MUTED, ha="left")

tier_legend = [
    Patch(facecolor=TEXT_MUTED, label="2025 (current)"),
    Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor=TEXT_MUTED, hatch="///", label="2055 (forecast)"),
    Patch(facecolor=lighten(TEXT_MUTED, 0.7), label="Full REMM capacity"),
]
fig.legend(handles=tier_legend, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=((LEFT + RIGHT) / 2, 0.82), ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, labelcolor=TEXT_MUTED, handlelength=1.5, columnspacing=1.2)

fig.text(0.97, 0.02, "Source: REMM 2055 run (WFRC)", fontsize=8, color=TEXT_MUTED, ha="right", style="italic")

plt.subplots_adjust(top=0.76, bottom=0.08, left=LEFT, right=RIGHT)
plt.savefig(output_dir / "employment_buildout.png", facecolor=fig.get_facecolor())
plt.show()
```

Same chart, for housing. Implemented as-is despite the known limitation
above: for Daybreak and Saratoga Springs Downtown, `housing_capacity` is
*less than* `housing_2055`, so the hatch overlay (2055) extends past the
light-shade track (capacity) instead of nesting inside it -- an honest
reflection of the density-assumption method understating real achievable
density there, not a rendering bug. `xmax` is taken as the max of both
`housing_capacity` and `housing_2055` (rather than just capacity, as in the
employment chart) so nothing gets clipped by this. Centers stay in the same
`order` as the employment chart (sorted by `jobs_capacity`) rather than
re-sorting by `housing_capacity`, so a center sits in the same row in both.

```{python}
xmax = max(summary["housing_capacity"].max(), summary["housing_2055"].max())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 5.9), dpi=140)
fig.patch.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
ax.set_facecolor(SURFACE)

for i, center in enumerate(order):
    hue = CENTER_COLORS[center]
    cap = summary.loc[center, "housing_capacity"]
    forecast = summary.loc[center, "housing_2055"]
    current = summary.loc[center, "housing_2025"]

    ax.barh(i, cap, height=bar_height, color=lighten(hue, 0.8), zorder=1)
    ax.barh(i, forecast, height=bar_height, facecolor="none", hatch="///", edgecolor=lighten(hue, 0.25), linewidth=0, zorder=2)
    ax.barh(i, current, height=bar_height, color=hue, zorder=3)

    top_y = i + bar_height / 2
    if current > 0:
        ax.text(current, top_y + 0.07, f"{current:,.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=TEXT_MUTED)
    else:
        ax.text(current, top_y + 0.07, "0", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=TEXT_MUTED)
    if not np.isclose(forecast, cap, rtol=0.001):  # skip only when 2055 == capacity (The Point) -- avoids a duplicate label
        ax.text(forecast, top_y + 0.07, f"{forecast:,.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=TEXT_MUTED)
    ax.text(cap + xmax * 0.015, i, f"{cap:,.0f}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=11, color=TEXT_PRIMARY, fontfamily="Poppins SemiBold")

ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)))
ax.set_yticklabels([CENTER_LABELS[c] for c in order], fontsize=11, color=TEXT_PRIMARY)
ax.set_xlim(0, xmax * 1.18)
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(order) - 1 + 0.75)
ax.get_xaxis().set_visible(False)

for spine in ax.spines.values():
    spine.set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)

fig.suptitle("Housing capacity across three WCV centers", x=0.03, y=0.975, fontsize=17, color=TEXT_PRIMARY, ha="left", fontfamily="Poppins SemiBold")
fig.text(0.03, 0.875, "Current homes (2025), REMM's 2055 forecast, and full buildout capacity", fontsize=11, color=TEXT_MUTED, ha="left")
fig.legend(handles=tier_legend, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=((LEFT + RIGHT) / 2, 0.82), ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, labelcolor=TEXT_MUTED, handlelength=1.5, columnspacing=1.2)
fig.text(0.97, 0.02, "Source: REMM 2055 run (WFRC)", fontsize=8, color=TEXT_MUTED, ha="right", style="italic")

plt.subplots_adjust(top=0.76, bottom=0.08, left=LEFT, right=RIGHT)
plt.savefig(output_dir / "housing_buildout.png", facecolor=fig.get_facecolor())
plt.show()
```
